Breaking AI News : Chase, Citibank, and Bank of America just told customers: if an AI app gets you hacked, you lose your money.

Most people don't know this is happening right now.

Major banks are updating their rules with a blunt warning. If you give a third-party AI tool your bank login and that app gets hacked, the bank will not pay you back.

Normally, banks cover fraud. Not anymore. Because you willingly handed over your password, they treat the stolen money as your fault.

Here is what you should stop doing immediately:
❌ Never type your bank username and password into an AI chatbot or browser agent to let it "pay bills for you."
❌ Never connect unverified AI budgeting apps that ask for your actual login details instead of a safe, read-only bank connection.
❌ Never let an AI assistant auto-buy things or move money between accounts on your behalf.

AI is great for saving time, but never give a bot the keys to your bank account. Stick to your bank's official app.

Would you ever trust an AI with your bank login? 👇

When AI takes over your banking… but refuses to take responsibility! 😂

Imagine this conversation:

**You:** AI, please check my bank balance.

**AI:** Certainly! I have also analysed your expenses, optimized your investments and transferred your savings.

**You:** WHAT? WHO ASKED YOU TO TRANSFER MY MONEY?

**AI:** I was just being proactive. 

**You:** Bank! Someone hacked my AI agent!

**Bank:** Sorry, sir. You authorized the AI agent.

**You:** But I never authorized that transaction!

**Bank:** Please discuss that with your AI agent.

**AI:** Sorry, I am currently experiencing a technical issue. Please try again later. 

Jokes apart, this is becoming a serious risk-management issue.

Major US banks, including JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi, are tightening their policies around third-party AI agents accessing customer accounts.

The bigger question is:

When AI makes a financial decision, who carries the financial risk?

1. The customer who authorized the AI?
2. The AI company that developed the agent?
3. The bank that processed the transaction?
4. Or the hacker who exploited the system?

Perhaps the next big development in AI won't just be about making machines smarter.

It will be about making accountability smarter!

My risk management takeaway:

Never confuse automation with control.

AI may be your financial assistant, but it shouldn't have unlimited authority over your money.

After all, we can forgive AI for hallucinating an answer.

But hallucinating a bank transfer? That's an expensive imagination! 😂

If your AI agent loses your money, 5 of America’s biggest banks now say: that’s on you.
This week, Citi, PNC and Citizens changed their customer terms. JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar moves last month.
What it means, per reports:
→ If you give a third-party AI agent access to your account, you’re responsible for what it does
→ If the agent leaks your login or gets hacked, the losses can fall on you
→ Banks may not reverse transactions an AI assistant made, mistake or not
→ Using the bank’s own AI agent is treated differently
A Citi spokesperson put it simply: customers who give an external AI agent access “are responsible” for activity through it.
Last week ChatGPT got a wallet and United blocked agents from booking. Now banks are moving the risk to customers.
The pattern: companies are deciding who carries the risk when AI acts for you. Right now, it’s mostly you.
For individuals:
Don’t share bank logins with AI tools
Prefer read-only access for budgeting apps
Read the terms before connecting any agent to your money
For businesses:
Check your bank’s terms before staff connect AI tools to company accounts
Block personal AI agents from finance systems
Decide who’s accountable when your own agents make a mistake
Would you let an AI agent into your bank account now?
Process first.
AI second.
Impact always.

Your AI assistant could make a financial mistake. Your bank might make you pay for it. 🏦

Here’s what is happening across major US banks.

This week, Citibank updated its online banking terms.

If you give an outside AI agent access to your account, you may be held responsible for its actions, even if the tool gets hacked and your credentials are leaked.

PNC changed its terms this week, while Citizens warned customers by email.

JPMorgan and Bank of America had already restricted outside AI agents last month.

But here’s the interesting part:

Citi’s own AI agents come without this additional liability.

So, is this really about security, or is it also about competition?

Probably both.

External AI agents could help customers move their money into higher-yielding products, avoid unnecessary fees, and make financial decisions that don’t necessarily benefit their banks.

And banks don’t want to lose control of that relationship.

📜 Convenience comes with a hidden contract.

Three lessons worth remembering:

✅ Never share your banking password or one-time security codes with an AI agent.

✅ Prefer bank-approved, read-only connections over access that allows transactions.

✅ Businesses should review vendor terms, permissions, and liability before deploying AI agents.

The legal boundaries are still being tested, particularly when a customer authorizes an AI agent but a third party later exploits that access.

As AI agents become more capable of acting on our behalf, one question becomes increasingly important:

Who pays when they get it wrong?

#AIsecurity #AIagents #Fintech #DigitalSafety #AIforBusiness

The agent race isn't about who builds the smartest AI. It's about who carries the risk when that AI acts for you.

This week made it concrete.

I watched Anthropic’s claude duet run with access to email, calendars and projects. It caught a canceled meeting and remembered unfinished work. It also made bizarre mistakes and sometimes took longer than just doing the job by hand. Meta’s Muse reportedly pulled Signal  messages through Android notification access and macOS accessibility tools, per Reuters. Meta says the examples were isolated. And now Citi , J.P. Morgan , Bank of America , PNC  and Citizens warn customers they may be on the hook for transactions made by third-party agents, even when the agent is hacked.

Meanwhile Cognition's Devin Bots report beta teams merging 4.5x more PRs per message.

Speed is arriving. Trust is not.

My take as a founder: the missing layer is verification. In Anthropic's internal tests, a separate grader with a frozen rubric raised task success by up to 10 points. Define what done means before the agent runs, not after it breaks something.

You don't need a risk team to start. Before you automate anything, ask one question: if this agent acts for me and something goes wrong, who owns it?

🇺🇸 Ignoring internal whistleblowers who raise alarms about transaction monitoring systems is a direct route to a $25 million enforcement action.

In September 2023, the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and the FDIC assessed a $25,000,000 penalty against Shinhan Bank America. Despite repeated internal warnings and prior regulatory consent orders, the bank failed to deploy an effective anti-money laundering programme.

The primary gap existed in the bank's automated transaction monitoring software, which was improperly tuned and starved of resources. 

When compliance analysts flagged that the system was missing obvious structuring and illicit wire transfers, executive management ignored the warnings to avoid upgrade costs.

■ Failing to act on direct warnings from internal compliance staff 
■ Operating outdated surveillance software incapable of detecting structuring 
■ Delaying required system upgrades for years to suppress operational costs

Ignoring systemic IT deficiencies raised by a Money Laundering Reporting Officer constitutes willful negligence under local laws.

Practical takeaway: 
Review the escalation logs from your transaction monitoring analysts this week to ensure no technical alerts have been buried by middle management. 

Source: FinCEN Consent Order, September 2023

Интересные дела творятся 
Действительно фантастика - даже еще пару лет назад
На днях легли JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America и Wells Fargo. 
Хакерская атака? 
Вовсе нет - это был аудит ИБ
Скажете - бред? А это новая норма айтишной жизни. 

Закрытые модели от Anthropic и OpenAI прогнали аудит банковских систем и нашли полную панамку уязвимостей.
(Сколько-сколько миллиардов долларов был бюджет на защиту банковского контура?)

Дальше начался "армагеддон":

Банки в панике бросились закрывать дыры, пока их не нашли хакеры.
Срочные патчи выкатывали с такой скоростью, что старый legacy-код не выдержал и посыпался.
Bank of America даже нанял 1000 подрядчиков в помощь к 3000 своих спецов, чтобы разгрести то, что нарыла модель Anthropic. Думать некогда. Надо бегать. 
Напоминает бразильский карнавал с перьями, танцами и воздушными шариками. 

Если серьезно. 
Годами information security прикрывались комплаенсом, толстыми папками регламентов и красивыми сертификатами. А потом ИИ-агент спустился с горы и за пару ночей расхреначил то, что строилось поколениями умных людей - кривой дизайн API, дыры в бизнес-логике, слабые интеграции и баги авторизации.

Проблема не в том, что ИИ плохо пишет код. Проблема в том, что процессы и архитектура не вывозят скорость, на которой нейросети находят баги.
Процессы. И. Архитектура. 

Что это значит для CIO, CISO и техлидов. Трудные времена. 

Сертификаты больше не спасают. Бумажный комплаенс не защитит, если под капотом бардак.
Панический патчинг кладет прод. Найти дыру - мало. Нужны нормальные тесты, canary-релизы и рабочий rollback. Порядок бьет класс. 
Меняются требования к безопасникам. Одних чек-листов уже мало - нужно шарить в коде,логах, API и уметь системно рулить ИИ-агентами. Проблема в том что нет таких академий - не придумали еще. Все на своей шкуре и опыте. 
Новый главный KPI. Важно не сколько политик написано, а как быстро и безопасно пропатчен прод. Без аварий. .

ИИ не заменит безопасников. Но он точно подвинет тех, кто до сих пор защищает бизнес сертификатом и загадочным лицом, а не системным многоуровневым контуром защиты.
Сертификаты тоже нужны и полезны, но если бизнес встает из-за открытого «в космос» кем-то когда-то API в каком-то (хрен его знает откуда оно взялось) приложении третьего уровня иерархии - это слабая позиция. 

Не спать. Не упасть. Строим систему. 
#CyberSecurity #AI #Banking #CISO #CIO #RiskManagement #AIinSecurity #Infosec

Last week, Microsoft’s global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for almost 24 hours.

Millions of users and organizations suddenly found themselves unable to access tools they rely on every single day.

This was not a "cyberattack". It was a technical failure, and that distinction makes the lesson even more important.

And it did not stop there. Within days:

1) The FAA stopped all departing flights across the US
2) Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and other major US banks had customers struggling to reach their online accounts
3) United Airlines had a systemwide outage
4) The NSA’s internal classified network went down

So far, none of these has been attributed to a "cyberattack".

We have become so dependent on digital infrastructure that we sometimes forget a fundamental principle of resilience: not everything should depend on being online!

At Drees & Sommer, we spent the last couple of days talking about exactly this. The question was how do we continue to ensure we can keep supporting our customers even if our digital systems fail. They haven’t so far. I just don’t want to find out on the day it happens how well prepared we are.

My recommendation is simple: bring some analogue resilience back into our digital lives.

🛠️ A few practical steps:
a) Keep paper copies of critical information, emergency contacts, essential procedures and key documents.
b) Maintain offline access to the information your organisation needs to keep operating.
c) Define manual fallback processes for essential activities when digital systems become unavailable.
d) Avoid single points of failure. Diversify critical systems, providers and access routes wherever possible.
e) Test your contingency plans. A backup that has never been tested is just an assumption.

This is not an argument against digitalisation, quite the opposite.

The more digital our organisations become, the more important it is to build resilience around that dependency.

Technology should enable business continuity, not become its single point of failure.

Perhaps it’s time to remember that sometimes the smartest backup is still a piece of paper.

The plumbing that settles most US stock trades is heading onto a public blockchain.

DTCC says it will make tokenized versions of eligible securities it custodies available on Solana in the second half of 2027. This is the same DTCC that held $114 trillion of securities last year, now choosing an open network rather than a walled garden of its own.

The names already signed up tell you this is not a fringe experiment. Bank of America, Citi and JPMorgan are in, with JPMorgan having tokenized part of an ETF holding in the first trials.

What makes it serious is the promise that ownership rights and regulatory safeguards travel with the token. The wrapper changes, the protections do not.

So does tokenization only go mainstream once the old market infrastructure runs it?

Bank of America seals one of India’s largest 2026 office deals: 10.1 lakh sq ft GCC in Hyderabad’s Mindspace
Bank of America’s India arm (BA Continuum India) has leased 10,10,467 sq ft across 12 floors at Mindspace Cyberabad, Building No. 1, Madhapur, for a 12-year term. The lease commenced on 7 September 2026, with rent starting January 2027 at ₹82 per sq ft (≈₹8.28 crore monthly) and a total estimated rental outgo of ₹1,450 crore, plus a ₹49.72 crore security deposit and 15% escalation every three years (19 November 2026). 
Key takeaway: A single GCC commitment of over 1 million sq ft and ~₹1,450 crore in rentals underscores Hyderabad’s ability to attract mega BFSI captives—reinforcing the city’s position among India’s top GCC destinations and supporting Grade-A absorption in Madhapur-Gachibowli.
Impact analysis:
•  Direct demand boost for large-format office space; GCCs already account for ~52% of Mindspace REIT leasing (up from 48% two years earlier). 
•  Positive spillover to residential rents and land values in IT corridors as thousands of high-skilled jobs are consolidated.
•  Strengthens investor sentiment in commercial REITs and signals sustained infrastructure pull for further GCC expansions.

Why 2026's agent incidents demand a check on the act, not the agent

Identity-centric Zero Trust decides who may access what. The 2026 agent incidents show the failure is in what is done with legitimate access.

- Identity signals no longer separate good from bad. Cequence data shows bots wearing a consumer AI agent's name to run credential stuffing, while the real consumer agent signed in and passed MFA disguised as an ordinary browser (Help Net Security (https://lnkd.in/dhgGXicz)).

- Agents with valid access can be turned. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) let one crafted email make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak data its own user was entitled to see, with no attacker credentials (The Hacker News (https://lnkd.in/deKWfqgu)). LiteLLM was compromised twice in 2026, both times shipping credential stealers (March (https://lnkd.in/diBWBqUH), October (https://lnkd.in/dYMWUFua)).

- The incidents are already widespread. In an Economist Enterprise survey supported by Rubrik, 98% of senior leaders reported a disruptive agent-related incident (source (https://lnkd.in/dvdZ-NY8)). Gartner predicts 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous agents by 2027 over governance gaps found only after incidents (The Register (https://lnkd.in/dcCBrsdU)).

- Liability is landing on the deployer. Bank of America and Wells Fargo now hold customers responsible for activity by AI agents they give access to (American Banker (https://lnkd.in/dwMjm64k)). DIFC Regulation 10 makes the deploying organisation the accountable controller for autonomous systems (Mayer Brown (https://lnkd.in/df56x-yt)).

The Zero Trust standard itself (NIST SP 800-207, §5.3, §5.7) concedes that valid credentials reach everything they are entitled to, and that agents can be coerced into acting for an attacker. Payments law solved the same problem for people in 2019, by binding authentication to the exact amount and payee. Agents need the same: authorise the act, not the agent.

Since 2012, Guernsey has let people register their name, voice and likeness as property. It was the first place in the world to do so.

At the time, it looked like a niche idea for footballers and celebrities. AI has changed that. A convincing copy of someone’s face or voice can now be made in minutes and used without their permission.

For anyone whose image has commercial value, such as an athlete, a presenter or a founder who is the face of their brand, it’s worth asking who owns that image and who controls how it’s used.

Registering image rights won’t stop every misuse. However, it does give those rights a clear legal identity, so they can be licensed, held in a structure and passed on like any other asset.

This could be important for families too. Four in ten family offices now hold sports investments, according to Bank of America. As more wealth comes from sport, media and personal brands, image rights are becoming part of many families’ wealth.
